title: Handoff notes between design and build
metaTitle: Notes a design file does not show
excerpt: Write what stays fixed, what may reflow, and what the empty and error states say. A link to a design file shows the happy path. It is not a handoff.
alt: A hand holding a blue pen over wireframe sketches, with a mug and a closed notebook nearby. The pen is writing the decision the frame cannot carry by itself.
caption: Sketches, and a pen still working. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What belongs in a design-to-development handoff?
faqs.answer: Write what is fixed, what may reflow at a smaller width, and what the empty, loading, error, and success states say. Include real copy lengths, the destination of each control, and focus for anything that is not only a hover. A frame of the happy path leaves the build to guess the rest.

faqs.question: Is a Figma or Zeplin link enough?
faqs.answer: The link can point at the frames. It does not replace a short note in the repository that states the rules and the open questions. Comments trapped in a tool the next person cannot open will not survive the build. Put the decisions next to the code, and link the frames from there.

faqs.question: How do you review the notes?
faqs.answer: Walk one flow, such as homepage to contact or product to confirmation, and check the error and the empty case at each step. Read the notes aloud to the person who will build. Every question they still have is a sentence the file is missing.

markdown:
Design to development handoff is a set of decisions the picture does not show. Write what is fixed, what may reflow, and what the empty, loading, and error states do. A link to a Zeplin file, or a Figma frame with no notes, is a tour of the happy path. The build starts where the happy path ends.

The person designing and the person building may be the same small team. The notes are still worth writing. In two weeks the frame will not remind you why the nav sticks, or what the form says when the network fails.

## What is fixed, and what may reflow

Fixed means the relationship you are protecting. The headline stays one sentence. The price stays next to the action. The logo stays in the corner you agreed. Reflow means the layout may change so those relationships survive a phone, a long translation, or a larger type size.

Say which one you mean for each region of the page. “This grid is four columns from this width up, and one column below. The order is the order in the frame.” “This hero may grow vertically. The button stays under the sentence, not over the photograph.” A developer should not have to infer the rule from a single desktop frame and a single mobile frame that happen to look tidy.

Write the type and space rules as tokens if you have them, or as a short list if you do not. Which text style is the headline, which is the quiet line, what the space is between sections. Hanabi’s builds use Tailwind on React and Next.js, with type and color decided in the design file first. The handoff should name those decisions so the code does not invent a third size because a frame was off by four pixels.

Call out anything that must not reflow. A comparison table that has to stay a table. A button label that must not wrap onto a joke of a third line. A crop that must keep a face. These constraints are cheap to write and expensive to discover after the component is “done.”

## States the frame usually skips

Every control that waits on a server has more than one face. Write them.

Empty: what a new account, an empty bag, or a filter with no results should say, and what action you offer. An empty screen with a blank illustration and no sentence is a dead end.

Loading: what moves, and what must not jump. If a skeleton is the choice, say which blocks it covers. If you would rather keep the layout still, say that. Motion in a Hanabi interface is there to explain a change, and it should respect a reduced-motion setting. Note that in the handoff so it is not a polish pass nobody scheduled.

Error: the sentence, where it appears, and what remains filled in. “We could not save this. Your text is still here.” Name the field when the field is the problem. The [W3C’s WCAG 2 overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) includes understandable errors and visible focus as part of a robust page. Put the actual copy in the note. “Show an error” is not copy.

Success: where they land, and what is repeated so they trust it worked. A toast that vanishes is not enough for a payment, a booking, or a file upload. Say if you need a page, an email, or both.

Disabled and permission: what a viewer sees when they cannot act, and why. A missing button looks like a bug. A button with “You need an editor role” is a state.

## Content, edges, and the things that break layouts

Give the real content, or a range you promise to support. The longest product name, the shortest, the headline with a real character, not “Lorem.” A layout that only works with the sample word will ship and then break on the first client edit.

Say what happens when a string is missing. If a subtitle is optional, the space should collapse. If an image is missing, say whether you show a fallback or hide the block. Do not leave the alt text as an afterthought in the component. Write the alt for the specific image, describing what is in it.

Images need a crop rule and a minimum size. “Cover the frame, keep the center” is a rule. “Make it nice” is a second design project during build. If art direction changes between mobile and desktop, provide both crops or say the focal point.

Links and buttons need the destination and the label as a pair. “Learn more” is not a handoff. “Read the shipping window, linking to /shipping” is a handoff. If a control opens a modal, say what the modal is for and how it closes. If it goes to another site, say so.

Forms need the field list, which are required, the validation rule in human language, and the request the form makes. Include the confirmation and the error you already wrote in the states section. A form without those is a picture of inputs.

## Interaction that is easy to miss

Hover is not a design. Anything that exists only on hover must exist another way for a person using a keyboard or a phone. Focus styles should be visible. If you designed a custom focus ring, put it in the file. If you did not, say that the browser default or the system default stays.

Sticky bars, hiding nav, and scroll tricks need a note about what they cover. A sticky purchase bar that covers the footer links, or the error on a form, is a defect you can predict. Write the z-order in a sentence: what stays on top, and what may scroll beneath.

Animation needs a limit. What moves, how far, and what happens when the person prefers reduced motion. A handoff that says “add some motion” will be interpreted differently by every engineer. Name the one moment that should move, such as the open of a menu, and leave the rest still.

Empty-looking frames are often component states in disguise. A selected tab, a current nav item, an active filter. Circle them and write the word. The build will otherwise style only the default and look finished in review.

## What the repository should receive

The handoff lands in the place the code lives, not only in a design tool’s comment thread. A short markdown file in the repo, next to the work, survives a lost Figma permission. Link the frames from that file. Do not replace the file with the link.

List the components you expect, in the names the team will use. A product card. A price block. A status line. Note which are new and which are the ones you already shipped, so the build extends the system instead of drawing a twin.

Include the tracking and the editable regions if the marketing team will change copy later. Which headlines are safe to edit in the CMS. Which sentences are structural and should not be casual afternoon edits. Payload or whatever you use is irrelevant if nobody marked the boundary.

Assets should be exported in the form the site will use, with names a person can search. Logo files for light and dark if you use both. Icons as the set you agreed, not as a screenshot. A client portal can hold the brand files after delivery. The repo still needs the ones the site actually loads.

Write the open questions at the bottom, dated. An open question is not a silent guess. If the price format is undecided, the engineer should not invent one at midnight. The note makes the gap visible so the founder can close it.

## A review that takes one sitting

Walk the notes against one flow, not against the whole company. Homepage to contact. Or product to bag to confirmation. For each step, check fixed versus reflow, the error, and the empty case. If a step has no sentence, stop and write it before implementation continues.

Read the notes aloud to the person who will build if you are not that person. The places they ask “what about…” are the places the file is still a picture. Add the answer to the file, not only to the call. If you are the same person, read the notes the next morning before you code. The gaps are easier to see after a night away from the frame you just drew.

Then look at a built page on a phone and on a keyboard, with one field intentionally broken. The handoff was honest if the error you wrote is the error you see, and if the layout holds with a long real title.

How those notes become a price is a different conversation. [How a studio estimates a marketing site](/blog/how-a-studio-estimates-a-marketing-site) is the next piece, because the states you just listed are a large part of what a page count leaves out.

When you want to see notes turn into an interface you can click, look through [Hanabi’s selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). The public projects are the result of decisions that had to be written down, not only framed.
